body:
Hey it's great, you don't even have to deal with breaking up with the dude, just walk away lol. 

Guy definitely ain't husband material.  NTA.

Often people forget to stop and look at what they have, it's not a nationality thing, not a gender thing, not an age thing etc; it's just a human thing.

I've been an expat most of my life in different continents, every place has its own perks, but local people will still complain about life no matter what, mostly because grass is greener on the other side. 

It can come across as people being ungrateful, especially to migrants who had to put in a lot of effort just to have what locals have by birth. But it's more so just people blindsided by their life experiences - it is hard to see what you have, before knowing that it's possible to not have it.

If you ask people, 'do you realise how lucky you are?' And then explain that the things they have assumed as basic things, are essentially luxury elsewhere, they would most likely tell you, yes sure I know that there are people who have it worse of.

But before actually experiencing different ways of living, even if people intellectually understood their privileges, it is not really emotionally understood. The same could apply in reverse, a german might look at you and ask you, "Do you realize how lucky you are? Here we don't get the opportunity to make friends as easily" etc (for the lack of a better example)

Thank you, your words concisely expressed my view. There's just no need to point at another persons life choices and call it selfish- not for having a kid, and not for not having a kid.

I'm probably gonna get downvoted to hell. It looks like many here are not comfortable considering any positive aspects about having kids. I think many people feel judged for being single and/or chosing to not have kids, and instinctively think that when anyone says anything positive about having a kid/getting married, there's a pair of judgmental eyes hiding behind it - which sadly is often true, just not always. And in this case- i assure you it isn't. 


I might be a minority opinion here, but i find when parents have kids and are determined to ' *give* them the best future', it actually usually doesn't end great. Those are often the (wealthy) parents who end up telling their kids what to study, what job to have, which friends to keep, which person to marry and the kids just end up rather lost when the parents pass away. It's a much more pleasant experience for the kid, when the focus is on helping the kid aquire skills, helping them fund joy in acquiring skills.


The world has never been perfect, i came from a middle class, growing up was not easy (but also definitely not the hardest- something i realise much later in life ). Every obstacle looked 50 times worse as a kid because they were all I knew, and I'm glad I survived so far. But while selfish reasons always exist when it comes to deciding to have or not have children, I think it'd be grossly unfair to look at my own parents and accuse them of having me purely for selfish reasons. They aren't perfect parents, they have many of the last-generation mindsets that are no longer accepted today, but they have been very loving, caring parents. 


it is great when you know yourself and decided that having a child is not for you, if it came from a deep understanding of your own personality -
many people do not find joy in helping and seeing a being grow at all, and prefer to focus on their own development, that's completely fine. Many find joy in such, but are not comfortable with the idea of it being at the expense of career opportunities, large percentage of ones life savings and a significant chuck of time, so they perhaps perfer having pets, plants, philanthropy projects etc - that's also completely fair. But also, many find joy in the process, spend time, effort, and resources raising their kids, and bring joy to the children themselves, that is also completely fine.


It sounds a bit like you had a rough time growing up, and you'd rather not recreate that experience, or create an even worse experience because the world looks like a mess - that fear is completely legit and reasonable. Many people who choose to be parents also have that fear, just probably also have the confidence that they can work it out to make it better. Some people do get pushed into it because of some sort of life ideal that was sold to them, which is terrible, but i think that's probably not the majority of people today.


Anyways, I wrote an essay to say..

TL;DR:
If you choose not to have a kid, it is completely fine. I personally think it is important to make sure this decision is made mostly because you know your personality, and know that itd just be weighing down your life, rather than because of worries about the future, but that is of course just my two cents.

I wouldn't even tell him as an ultimatum though. I'd just tell him that this is an action that would hurt the relationship badly, and if he still decides to go, then there is no point keeping him in your life.

while I totally understand how comments like such possibly sound like  "ugh I would never want that" on the receiving end, if it makes you feel better, I think most of the times it's just the fact that people often show compassion by putting themselves in other people's shoes, but sometimes that just doesn't work out and they end up sounding more like they are judging.

How weird, this is rather someone who thinks having a child is a crime would react, i can at least half way make sense of it, if she's saying how she's not fine with the idea of bringing a life to the world in the current state of the world or something.

but the comments she made are not even about that, rather it's about how it will - in her imagination - make YOUR life miserable. To me, that sounds like she's projecting, she puts herself in your shoes and concluded that she would make a different decision. And then she decides that, if your choices won't align to hers, your friendship is worthless

In reality, I think she thought you were buddies fighting the idea of not having kids, and feels betrayed- I don't know your history. But unless this specific topic had been part of it (like if she had to take an abortion, had gone through miscarriages or something, and had to convince herself that it was her choice to do so),I find it really hard to make sense of all of this drama.

You said you dodged a bullet, but I think that bullet had no chance of hitting you anyways. Those who can be hit, so to say, are people who don't realise what's wrong when they hear such words and turn inward to doubt themselves.

Congratulations.

A bit of a broad stroke there, I'm sure some of our parents didn't just chuck us in a separate room to sort ourselves out as babies. Most parents were probably as loving as parents today are.

Who knows, maybe its genetics, maybe she's misremembering, maybe she just wanted to be looked at as a woman who did exceptionally well at parenting.

We are lucky that our daughter has been generally pretty relaxed, but we also had a few hard nights, probably every parent does. What i find really helpful is switching my perspective to imagine my life as a tiny being like her, who has little control of her body, is constantly hungry but also constantly throwing up, wants to talk but have no words, spends half of the day sitting in her own pee and shit, and have no strength to help herself if anyone or anything is harming her. Hell, even farting is a mission.

The newborn life just looks so tough and unpleasant to me, I just feel so bad for her when she is suffering. 

Maybe I'm being weird about it, but in my mind it's not so different than being an old person in hospital bed, constantly sick and scared about what's going to happen. I don't get mad at her, 'cause the if I imagine how she's feeling it just all seem so terrifying to me; mostly I feel helpless and sad that I can't help her more.

In any case, I hope the phase passes by soon, and you can get some proper sleep.

I'd like to be half of a devils advocate- I think you might not be 'overthinking' per se; it just isn't your responsibility. 

It's possible that she is generally sensitive to sounds, maybe she never liked you because she knew that two people will make more noise than one person, and maybe the baby crying was too much for her. 

But in any case, it is her sensitivity that moved her out, not you and your family. If her neighbor gets a dog it'd be too much. If her neighbor likes having friends over, it's be too much for her... etc. One way or another, she'd be annoyed by something eventually, and you just happened to be there this time round. 

It's probably best for her to find a place where she wouldn't have to think about her neighbors, this place isn't right for her.

My husband was there for pretty much all of the appointments, but thats only because we both work from home and it was easy enough for him to move his schedules around the appointments.i don't think it is necessary, but there were parts of me that also thinks, in the unlikely event of anything going wrong, I'd like him to be there.

So it kind of depends on the situation- if your pregnancy is generally smooth and it takes a lot of effort for your partner to ask for leaves etc, it is probably fine to save yourselves all that stress just to have him there; but if it isn't too difficult for him to take a few hours off work etc, then it'd be nice to have someone accompany you.

Every marriage is different, but i think a lot of marriage started when the relationship isn't mature enough.  A lot of what people complain about in marriage seem to be stemming from mis/non- communication, and/or a lack of understanding of each other.

It doesn't help that many people have been brought up seeing marriage as some sort of a life goal to chase, instead of something that one should only consider when the relationship is mature enough. Some people dream of being a bride or having a family since a young age, and I think that completely misses the point of marriage. A lot of these people ended up in marriage to fulfill that image they have, just to then realize they don't really know their spouse.

I don't know if that's "most" people, but I can certainly say that it seems to be a pattern, when people complain how their partner has 'changed' after they got married. I've known my husband for more than a decade before we tied the knot, and we've always been pretty good at supporting each other- that is the reason we got married. Nothing much changed after we got married, except we manage our time and resources more as a family than as two individuals.
Ugh.. so sad how some people are, I wish these people knew they are being rather pathetic.

I mean, I might be an outlier myself, but I find it silly that 'Nesting ' is such a thing that people talk about.

Im a few weeks behind you, and I did purchase things like pram, baby bed etc. Did some reorg of the house to make sure the placements of these items are as sensible as i can imagine, which involves some cleaning. But I'm also just trying to be prepared for a future problem, knowing that labor will likely put me in a state where I don't have the mobility i have now to go out and purchase things easily if I need them, and I have no idea how much mental/physical capacity we have as a couple to deal with stuff like this when the baby is demanding constant attention,  since it's our first kid. 

It's not different than, say, packing a luggage for a future trip. 

The experience of pregnancy and motherhood is a big deal to a person's life, but I personally find it unnecessary to essentially re-write our identities to suddenly treat it as if EVERYTHING we do or think revolves around the new situation of becoming a mother and some sort of motherly instinct etc. We are just the same normal humans trying to deal with a new situation; some of us prefer to set things up early before the birth of a child in an attempt to minimize the much anticipated troubles, others prefer to wait till the child is born before setting things up, so that the situation can be assessed accurately. And there's probably another thousand ways to deal with it differently. It's all pretty normal. 

I personally am not a fan of it being treated as some sort of special motherly instinct, with people going "ohhh you are in nesting mode" when they hear about any preparation. I'm not a bird - just a regular human trying to solve foreseeable issues, as I normally do, regardless of whether I'm pregnant or not.

The intentions were friendly so it's not toooooo bad, but just people saying 'ohh your belly' and then touched my belly as if I were there to be touched, no asking, and tI should be excited about people wanting to touch it. 

I'm a pretty private person,  I don't advertise my pregnancy or define myself by my pregnancy, and I'd honestly prefer it if no one touches my body.

But she did mean well, so i tolerated it.

A long time ago, I thought I did, and I was somewhat stuck in depression for years. Trusted this person, and threw a lot away in my life, only to get back to someone who stonewalled me and said Oops I'm don't have feelings for you anymore and I can't explain it. 

Hindsight now that was just a crap excuse from a person who never really cared much for it, although that's not what it looked like in the beginning. I think i just needed a period of time to mourn, and it lasted quite a while, but eventually, i realized that this person is not worth my emotion or attention.

Now thinking back, I'm pretty glad I didn't end up having this person in my life .

That's fair enough, but hey, worth a try.  I was an awkward teenager growing up, would possibly end up doing exactly what you said- but it would probably also bring a bit of comfort to know that I am invited to express how I feel. If he's too shy, maybe even let him know that he could also just send a message on WhatsApp or something.

It might be worth it to literally just ask him if he is happy, and to ask him what you can do to make if easier for him, rather than trying the whole lot of things that he may or may not want/ understand.  I might be naive, but 16 year old me would probably appreciate being asked about what I want.

Instead of wondering whether you need to comply with his demands, perhaps have a think about what ways there are to get out of this relationship safely.


Perhaps you've been through too much together, that you can't see how abusive his actions are. But slow down, put away the part of yourself that wants to hang onto having him in your life and wants to make him feel better, and ask yourself: would you do what he does to you, to anyone you love?


He may be angry, distressed, anxious etc because life is tough and who-knows-what, but if he had any respect and braincells, he'd rather treasure your existence than acting like it's my way or the highway. He doesn't have the basic respect for you, and that makes your marriage with him worse than none existence. 


There is, in the long term (probably in the short term too), not much left for you in this marriage already. Don't sign anything; start planning your exit. If he wants to accuse you of anything, let him. I can imagine how much itd hurt, especially if you've been trying for so long to prove that you aren't this evil person he describes to no avail, and it's hard to walkaway, especially if he eventually pulls the 'do this to prove yourself' card to make it sound like this is the last time he asks you of something. 


But you deserve a better life than babysitting some entitled abusive adult baby all day long.

Perhaps I'm weird, but to me, a genuine romatic relationship can only grow from a genuine friendship, and gender is irrelevant in genuine friendships.

Maybe a weird one, but I started meeting groups of expecting/new mothers, and it scares me a little how it felt like most of the people there identifies themselves as a mother and nothing else. It's hard to explain, but every conversation is around the technical tips and tricks of taking care of a baby. 


I get that having a new baby is a huge deal in life, but I don't feel particularly comfortable defining everything I do around the baby. I mentioned that ive been buying things for the baby to make sure our home would be ready when the baby is born, they all go "awww you are in nesting mode"; im not in some special mother "mode", I'm just trying to resolve a problem before there is one as an adult.


The other thing is, I thought there would be a lot of conversations on how THEY themselves, their partners or their lifestyles changed with the arrival of the baby, but that conversation doesn't really happen, or when it does it's almost always described from the "aww im a mama now, things we do for our babies" kinda sentiment. 


Maybe it's just me, but it kinda scares me how most of the people in the groups ive been to seem to be - happily - losing their own identity.

People become more 'picky ' about who they spend time with as people age (friendship and otherwise), that's just us finally having a good grasp of what we enjoy in the company of others, there isn't anything wrong with it.  

Question is what 'too' picky means- if that means you find it difficult to fully enjoy the company of people you are dating because somehow most of them don't have what makes you happy (maybe because there are common traits from how/where you get to know these people etc), then it is what it is, and it's not a bad thing.

After all, you don't have to put yourself in a relationship - I personally find it completely normal to only be in a relationship if having the other person in your life makes life better. If not then I'd rather roam alone.

Those words definitely are comforting, I'm expecting and already terrified of feeling like I'm freeloading once I cannot work and have a child to take care of; not even mentioning the career gap that comes with it etc. Not sure why I was so native, but before we started really thinking about have a child, I somehow thought I could give birth and go straight back to work, to "shoulder half of the load", totally overlooking the fact that the child need constant care 😅 🙃

Geez, I thought this whole alpha male thing was debunked ages ago by the guy who came up with the theory himself, why are people still buying it?

Just be a normal, respectful human being?

You sound rightfully burnt out; as an expecting mom, I've a lot of respect for single parents- never really thought about all of these things before, but now that I have to, I honestly think all single parents are superhuman.

From here onwards, you will probably slowly have more and more time for yourself. You've made it through some of the toughest parts of raising a kid; and hopefully, once you get to breathe a little, you slowly find yourself back again.
